name: Capsaicin (applied to the skin)
short: Burning on application is common: risk ratio 5.56 in osteoarthritis trials. The 8% patch causes intense initial burning; in its trials, serious adverse events were similar to control.
text: Applied to the skin, capsaicin first causes enhanced sensitivity, followed by reduced sensitivity and, with repeated use, desensitisation. In a Cochrane review of six trials (389 participants) of low-concentration (0.075%) cream applied regularly for neuropathic pain, local skin reactions were more common with capsaicin (number needed to harm 2.5), usually tolerable and lessening with time, although skin irritation may lead to withdrawal; systemic adverse effects were rare. A meta-analysis of eight randomised trials in osteoarthritis (498 patients, capsaicin 0.0125% to 5%) found that capsaicin may increase burning at the application site (risk ratio 5.56; number needed to harm 3; five studies). The high-concentration 8% patch must be applied under highly controlled conditions, often after a local anaesthetic, because of the intense initial burning it causes; in a Cochrane review of eight trials (2488 participants), six of which used 0.04% capsaicin as the control, local adverse events were common but not consistently reported, serious adverse events were no more common with the patch (3.5%) than with control (3.2%), withdrawals for adverse events did not differ, and no deaths were judged to be related to the study medication. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
